author: Amanda Faith
title: My Life Felt Completely Out of Control-Here's How I Started Finding My Way Back - NewsBreak
text:
By Amanda Faith ,
21 hours ago
There was a stretch where everything felt like it was happening to me instead of with me. My days were packed, my brain was loud, and even small decisions felt weirdly high-stakes. Nothing was “one big crisis,” but the constant churn made it hard to trust myself or feel steady.
What helped wasn’t a dramatic overhaul. It was a series of grounded moves that made my life feel workable again—one small decision at a time. Here’s what I started doing, and why it made such a difference.
Take stock of what’s actually controllable When life feels chaotic, it’s easy to treat everything as urgent and equally solvable. I started by separating what I could influence today (my schedule, my boundaries, my next step) from what I couldn’t (other people’s reactions, past decisions, the pace of the world). That simple sorting reduced the mental load right away.
A practical way to do this is a two-column list: “Mine to act on” and “Not mine to carry.” The second column isn’t denial—it’s permission to stop spending energy where it won’t change the outcome. Once I saw the controllables clearly, I could focus my effort instead of scattering it.
Build one “anchor” routine and protect it I didn’t have the bandwidth for a full morning routine, a workout plan, a new diet, and a meditation streak all at once. So I picked one anchor that made me feel more like myself and repeated it daily. Sometimes it was a short walk, sometimes it was ten minutes of planning, sometimes it was making a real breakfast.
The point wasn’t perfection; it was stability. An anchor routine creates a reliable reference point in your day, especially when everything else shifts. Over time, it becomes proof that you can keep a promise to yourself—even on messy days.
Reduce decisions by making a few things automatic When I felt overloaded, even minor choices—what to eat, when to respond, what to tackle first—could drain me. I started automating the repeatable stuff: a simple grocery list I could rotate, a default weekday breakfast, a set time to check messages, a few “go-to” outfits. Less decision-making meant more energy for what actually needed my attention.
This isn’t about rigid rules; it’s about removing friction. If your brain is already running hot, you don’t need to negotiate with yourself about every small thing. A few defaults can create breathing room surprisingly fast.
Set boundaries that match your real capacity I used to set boundaries based on who I wanted to be on my best day. Then a normal day would arrive, and I’d blow past my limits trying to keep up. The shift happened when I started basing “yes” and “no” on my actual capacity—sleep, workload, stress level, and what I needed to stay functional.
Simple scripts helped: “I can’t take that on this week,” “I need more time to answer,” or “I’m not available for that.” Boundaries aren’t a personality trait; they’re logistics. When I treated them like practical guardrails, I stopped feeling guilty and started feeling safer.
Get specific about the next step (not the whole plan) When everything feels out of control, the temptation is to fix your entire life in one giant plan. That only made me freeze. What helped was narrowing down to the next concrete step—something I could do in 10–20 minutes that moved one problem forward.
Instead of “get finances together,” it became “open the banking app and list bills due this week.” Instead of “fix my health,” it became “schedule a checkup” or “take a 15-minute walk.” Small steps create momentum, and momentum makes the future feel less threatening.
Reconnect with support in a practical way I didn’t always need a deep heart-to-heart, but I did need connection that made life easier. Sometimes that meant asking a friend to sit with me while I sorted paperwork, or telling someone, “I’m not doing great—can we talk for ten minutes?” Making it specific lowered the barrier to reaching out.
If you’ve got access to professional support, that can matter, too—especially when overwhelm starts affecting sleep, work, relationships, or your ability to function. The key for me was dropping the idea that I had to “earn” help by being in the worst possible state. Support works best early, when things are wobbly, not shattered.
Getting back to steady didn’t happen in one breakthrough moment. It came from choosing a few stabilizing habits and repeating them until my nervous system started to believe I was safe again. If you’re in that spun-out place, start small and stay honest—tiny, consistent steps are often what bring your life back within reach.
